questions.q: Which of the following plants is pollinated by water?
questions.explanation: Vallisneria is a water-pollinated plant; maize is wind-pollinated and Salvia and rose are insect-pollinated.

questions.q: The formation of seeds without fertilisation is called:
questions.explanation: Apomixis is a form of asexual reproduction that mimics sexual reproduction by producing seeds without fertilisation.

questions.q: The embryo sac of a flowering plant develops from which structure?
questions.explanation: One megaspore of the tetrad is functional; its nucleus divides mitotically to form the 8-nucleate embryo sac.

questions.q: Which highly resistant organic material is present in the exine of the pollen grain?
questions.explanation: Sporopollenin is one of the most resistant organic materials and withstands high temperature, strong acids and alkalis.

questions.q: Self-incompatibility in plants helps to prevent self-pollen from fertilising the ovules because it:
options: Stops entry of foreign pollen into the stigma
Inhibits germination or growth of self-pollen tube in the pistil
Prevents formation of the embryo sac
questions.explanation: Self-incompatibility is a genetic mechanism in which the pistil rejects pollen of the same flower or plant, promoting out-breeding.

questions.q: After the pollen tube enters the ovule through the micropyle, it releases the two male gametes into which cell of the embryo sac?
questions.explanation: The pollen tube enters one synergid through the filiform apparatus and discharges the male gametes there.

questions.q: Describe the structure of the wall of a mature pollen grain.
questions.answer: A pollen grain has a two-layered wall. The hard outer exine is made of sporopollenin and has germ pores where sporopollenin is absent. The inner intine is a thin continuous layer of cellulose and pectin.
keyPoints: Inner intine of cellulose and pectin
questions.explanation: Sporopollenin makes pollen well preserved as fossils.

questions.q: Why are emasculation and bagging done in artificial hybridisation?
questions.answer: Emasculation removes the anthers from a bisexual flower before they dehisce, which prevents self-pollination. Bagging covers the flower with a bag to prevent contamination of its stigma by unwanted pollen; the bag is removed after the desired pollen is dusted.
keyPoints: Bagging prevents contamination by unwanted pollen
questions.explanation: These steps ensure that only the chosen male parent pollinates the female parent.

questions.q: Which hormone is secreted mainly by the corpus luteum?
questions.explanation: The corpus luteum secretes large amounts of progesterone, which maintains the endometrium for implantation.

questions.q: The acrosome at the head of a sperm contains:
options: Hydrolytic enzymes that help the sperm penetrate the egg covering
questions.explanation: The acrosome is a cap-like structure filled with enzymes that help fertilisation.

questions.q: The process by which spermatids are transformed into spermatozoa is called:
questions.explanation: Spermiogenesis is the transformation of spermatids into sperms; spermiation is the release of sperms from Sertoli cells into the lumen.

questions.q: Entry of more than one sperm into the ovum is prevented by changes in the:
questions.explanation: Contact of a sperm with the zona pellucida induces changes that block the entry of additional sperms.

questions.q: Which statement about the human blastocyst is correct?
options: The inner cell mass attaches to the endometrium
A blastocyst forms at the zygote stage
The trophoblast attaches to the endometrium and the inner cell mass differentiates into the embryo
questions.explanation: The trophoblast layer helps in implantation, and the inner cell mass gives rise to the embryo.

questions.q: In a woman with a regular 28-day menstrual cycle, ovulation typically takes place about:
questions.explanation: Ovulation occurs near the middle of the cycle, around day 14, after the LH surge.

questions.q: Differentiate between spermatogenesis and oogenesis in any three points.
questions.answer: Spermatogenesis begins at puberty and continues throughout life, whereas oogenesis begins in the foetus and ovulation starts at puberty and stops at menopause. One spermatogonium gives four functional sperms, while one oogonium gives one ovum and polar bodies. Spermatogenesis occurs in testes and oogenesis in ovaries.
keyPoints: Spermatogenesis starts at puberty, oogenesis starts before birth
Four sperms versus one ovum and polar bodies
questions.explanation: Oogenesis includes arrested stages that complete only after sperm entry.

questions.q: Outline the events from fertilisation to the implantation of the embryo in the uterus.
questions.answer: The zygote undergoes mitotic cleavage as it moves through the fallopian tube, forming 2, 4, 8 and 16 blastomeres, called a morula. The morula becomes a blastocyst with an outer trophoblast and an inner cell mass. The trophoblast attaches to the endometrium and the blastocyst is implanted.
keyPoints: Cleavage forms blastomeres and a morula
Morula becomes a blastocyst (trophoblast and inner cell mass)
Trophoblast attaches to the endometrium: implantation
questions.explanation: Implantation leads to the formation of the placenta.

questions.q: Which of the following sexually transmitted infections is caused by a bacterium?
questions.explanation: Gonorrhoea is caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae, whereas the other three are viral.

questions.q: The technique in which ova from the female and sperms from the male are fused outside the body and the embryo is transferred is commonly known as:
questions.explanation: In vitro fertilisation followed by embryo transfer is popularly called the test tube baby programme.

questions.q: Intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) is a technique in which:
options: An ovum is transferred into the fallopian tube
Semen is introduced into the vagina
An embryo is transferred into the uterus
A sperm is injected directly into an ovum
questions.explanation: ICSI is an assisted reproductive technique in which a sperm is directly injected into the ovum in the laboratory.

questions.q: Oral contraceptive pills prevent pregnancy mainly by:
options: Inhibiting ovulation and implantation and altering the quality of cervical mucus
Killing all sperms in the testis
questions.explanation: Hormonal pills inhibit ovulation and implantation and alter cervical mucus to retard the entry of sperms.

questions.q: Emergency contraceptives such as progestogens or IUDs are most effective if used within what time of unprotected coitus?
questions.explanation: They are effective if administered within 72 hours of coitus and are meant only for emergency use.

questions.q: Which single method gives protection against both unwanted pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections?
questions.explanation: A condom acts as a barrier and prevents contact with semen and body fluids that carry pathogens.

questions.q: What is amniocentesis? State two legitimate uses.
questions.answer: Amniocentesis is a prenatal diagnostic technique in which a sample of the amniotic fluid containing foetal cells is withdrawn and analysed. It can detect chromosomal abnormalities such as Down's syndrome and certain metabolic disorders in the foetus.
keyPoints: Analysis of amniotic fluid with foetal cells
questions.explanation: The test is legally banned for determining foetal sex.

questions.q: Suggest three measures to check the rapid growth of the human population.
questions.answer: Create awareness about small family norms and the use of contraceptives, and educate people about reproductive health. Statutory raising of the marriageable age (18 for females and 21 for males) and incentives for small families also help.
keyPoints: Awareness of small families and contraception
Incentives for couples with small families
questions.explanation: A falling death rate and rising birth rate have caused a population explosion in India.

questions.q: The different forms of a gene that occupy the same locus on homologous chromosomes are called:
questions.explanation: Alleles are alternative forms of a gene, such as T and t for height in pea.

questions.q: Which pair of sex chromosomes is present in a normal human male?
questions.explanation: Human males are heterogametic with X and Y chromosomes, and females have XX.

questions.q: A woman who is a carrier of colour blindness (X-linked recessive) marries a man with normal vision. What proportion of their sons is expected to be colour blind?
questions.explanation: XCXc x XCY gives sons XCY and XcY in equal numbers, so half the sons are colour blind.

questions.q: Down's syndrome is caused by:
questions.explanation: An extra copy of chromosome 21 causes Down's syndrome.

questions.q: For an X-linked recessive disease, an affected father marries a normal homozygous mother. Their children will be:
options: Half of the daughters carriers and half affected
All daughters carriers and all sons normal
questions.explanation: Sons receive the Y from the father and a normal X from the mother; daughters receive the father's affected X and a normal X, so they are carriers.

questions.q: A child has the karyotype 44 autosomes + XXY. The child is:
questions.explanation: The presence of an extra X chromosome in a male (47, XXY) is Klinefelter's syndrome, due to non-disjunction of sex chromosomes.

questions.q: What is pleiotropy? Give an example.
questions.answer: Pleiotropy is the phenomenon in which a single gene affects more than one phenotypic trait. An example is phenylketonuria, in which a mutation in the gene for phenylalanine hydroxylase causes mental retardation, reduced hair and skin pigmentation.
questions.explanation: Pleiotropy contrasts with polygenic inheritance, where many genes control one trait.

questions.q: Why is the inheritance of ABO blood groups an example of both multiple allelism and codominance?
questions.answer: The ABO gene has three alleles, IA, IB and i, and this is multiple allelism. IA and IB are both dominant over i, and when they occur together in a person (IAIB) both are expressed equally, producing group AB, which is codominance.
keyPoints: Three alleles IA, IB and i
IA and IB are both expressed in AB individuals
questions.explanation: Any person carries only two of the three alleles.

questions.q: The double helix model of DNA was proposed by:
questions.explanation: James Watson and Francis Crick proposed the double helix model in 1953 based on X-ray diffraction data.

questions.q: The Human Genome Project was declared complete in which year?
questions.explanation: The project was launched in 1990 and completed in 2003.

questions.q: Introns of the primary transcript (hnRNA) in eukaryotes are:
questions.explanation: Introns are non-coding sequences removed by splicing, and exons are joined to form mRNA.

questions.q: In their experiment on semi-conservative replication, Meselson and Stahl grew E. coli in a medium containing:
questions.explanation: The heavy isotope 15N made the DNA denser, so it could be separated from 14N DNA by caesium chloride density gradient centrifugation.

questions.q: E. coli grown for many generations in 15N medium is transferred to 14N medium. After two generations, the DNA will be:
questions.explanation: After one generation all DNA is hybrid; after two, half is hybrid and half is light because replication is semi-conservative.

questions.q: A double-stranded DNA segment has 20% adenine. What is the percentage of guanine in it?
questions.explanation: A = T = 20%, so A + T = 40%; the remaining 60% is G + C, so G = 30%.

questions.q: Write any three differences between DNA and RNA.
questions.answer: DNA has deoxyribose sugar, but RNA has ribose. DNA contains thymine while RNA contains uracil. DNA is generally double-stranded and stable, while RNA is usually single-stranded and more reactive.
questions.explanation: The 2'-OH in RNA makes it more reactive and less stable.

questions.q: Explain why tRNA is called the adapter molecule in protein synthesis.
questions.answer: A tRNA has an anticodon loop that reads the codon on mRNA by base pairing, and an amino acid acceptor end that carries a specific amino acid. So it links the nucleotide language of mRNA to the amino acid sequence of the protein.
keyPoints: Anticodon pairs with the mRNA codon
questions.explanation: Crick called it the adapter in his hypothesis.

questions.q: The theory of natural selection was put forward by:
questions.explanation: Charles Darwin proposed natural selection as the mechanism of evolution in 'On the Origin of Species'.

questions.q: The mutation theory of evolution, which suggests that large single-step mutations cause speciation, was proposed by:
questions.explanation: Hugo de Vries, working on evening primrose, proposed that mutations (saltations) are the cause of evolution.

questions.q: The age of fossils is estimated mainly by:
questions.explanation: Radioactive isotopes of known half-lives in the rocks or fossils are used to estimate their age.

questions.q: The first human-like hominid, which probably ate fruits and had a brain capacity of 650-800 cc, was:
questions.explanation: Homo habilis had a brain capacity between 650 and 800 cc and probably did not eat meat.

questions.q: Why do bacteria become resistant after repeated exposure to an antibiotic?
options: The antibiotic converts bacteria into resistant forms
Pre-existing resistant mutants survive and multiply under selection pressure
The bacteria use the antibiotic as food
questions.explanation: The antibiotic acts as a selective agent; resistant variants leave more offspring, so the resistant fraction rises.

questions.q: A few individuals from a large population establish a new colony, and its allele frequencies differ from the original population by chance. This is called:
questions.explanation: The founder effect is a type of genetic drift in which the founders carry only a random sample of the parent population's alleles.

questions.q: What is convergent evolution? Give an example.
questions.answer: Convergent evolution is the development of similar adaptive functional structures in unrelated groups of organisms living in similar environments. An example is the Australian marsupials and the corresponding placental mammals, such as the marsupial mole and the placental mole.
keyPoints: Example: Australian marsupials and placental mammals
questions.explanation: Convergent evolution produces analogous structures.

questions.q: Describe stabilising, directional and disruptive natural selection.
questions.answer: In stabilising selection more individuals acquire the mean character value, so the peak becomes narrower. In directional selection individuals of one extreme are favoured, so the peak shifts in one direction. In disruptive selection both extremes are favoured, producing two peaks in the distribution.
keyPoints: Stabilising: mean value favoured, narrower peak
Directional: one extreme favoured, peak shifts
Disruptive: both extremes favoured, two peaks
questions.explanation: These are the three ways natural selection can affect a population's distribution.

questions.q: Dengue fever is transmitted by which mosquito?
questions.explanation: Dengue is a viral disease spread by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus.

questions.q: Antibodies produced by B lymphocytes are chemically:
questions.explanation: Antibodies are protein molecules (immunoglobulins) made of two light and two heavy chains.

questions.q: Which antibody class is mainly associated with allergic responses?
questions.explanation: IgE binds to mast cells, which release histamine and serotonin, causing allergic symptoms.

questions.q: Interferons, which protect non-infected cells from further viral infection, are secreted by:
questions.explanation: Virus-infected cells secrete interferons, which are part of cellular barriers of innate immunity.

questions.q: Heroin (smack) is chemically:
questions.explanation: Heroin is diacetylmorphine, obtained by acetylation of morphine, which is extracted from the latex of the poppy plant.

questions.q: The RNA genome of HIV is copied into DNA after the virus enters a host cell, and this DNA is inserted into the host DNA. Which enzyme catalyses the copying?
questions.explanation: HIV is a retrovirus; reverse transcriptase makes viral DNA from RNA, which integrates into the host genome.

questions.q: Name the two types of lymphocytes involved in the adaptive immune response and state their roles.
questions.answer: B-lymphocytes produce antibodies in the blood (humoral immune response). T-lymphocytes do not secrete antibodies but help B cells produce them and mediate the cell-mediated immune response, such as in graft rejection.
keyPoints: T cells help B cells and give cell-mediated immunity
questions.explanation: Cell-mediated immunity is responsible for graft rejection.

questions.q: How does a vaccine differ from an antiserum? Give an example of each use.
questions.answer: A vaccine contains weakened or killed pathogens or their antigenic proteins, which stimulate the body to make antibodies and memory cells, giving active immunity (e.g. polio vaccine). An antiserum contains ready-made antibodies and gives quick passive immunity, as in tetanus or snake bite.
keyPoints: Vaccine: antigens give active immunity and memory
Antiserum: ready-made antibodies give passive immunity
Examples: polio vaccine; antiserum for snake bite or tetanus
questions.explanation: Antiserum is used when immediate protection is required.

questions.q: The large holes in Swiss cheese are due to:
options: Carbon dioxide produced by Propionibacterium sharmanii
questions.explanation: A large amount of CO2 produced by the bacterium Propionibacterium sharmanii forms the large holes.

questions.q: The dough used for making bread rises because of:
options: Carbon dioxide produced by baker's yeast
questions.explanation: Baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) ferments sugars and releases CO2, which puffs up the dough.

questions.q: Which one is a free-living, nitrogen-fixing aerobic bacterium used as a biofertiliser?
questions.explanation: Azotobacter and Azospirillum are free-living nitrogen fixers; Rhizobium is symbiotic.

questions.q: Which bacterium is used as a biological control agent against butterfly caterpillars?
questions.explanation: Bacillus thuringiensis spores are mixed with water and sprayed on plants, where caterpillars eat them and die.

questions.q: In secondary treatment of sewage, the effluent is passed into aeration tanks and air is pumped continuously. This is done because:
options: It promotes vigorous growth of aerobic microbes that form flocs and consume organic matter
It kills all the bacteria in the effluent
It removes the large floating debris
It increases the BOD of the effluent
questions.explanation: Aerobic microbes form flocs and decompose organic matter, reducing the BOD of the effluent.

questions.q: In a biogas plant, the final production of methane from organic matter is carried out by:
questions.explanation: Methanogens grow anaerobically on cellulosic material and produce methane along with CO2 and H2.

questions.q: What is fermentation? Name two products obtained by microbial fermentation.
questions.answer: Fermentation is the metabolic breakdown of organic substances by microbes in the absence of oxygen, giving products such as organic acids or alcohol. Examples are ethanol from Saccharomyces cerevisiae and lactic acid by Lactobacillus.
keyPoints: Microbial breakdown of substrate, usually anaerobic
Products like ethanol and lactic acid
questions.explanation: Large-scale fermentation is done in fermentors.

questions.q: Why are baculoviruses (nucleopolyhedroviruses) considered suitable for integrated pest management?
questions.answer: They attack insects and other arthropods and are species-specific with narrow spectrum insecticidal action. They have no negative effects on plants, mammals, birds, fish or even non-target insects, which is useful for ecologically sensitive areas.
keyPoints: No harmful effect on non-target organisms
Useful in integrated pest management and sensitive areas
questions.explanation: Integrated pest management aims at reducing chemical pesticides.

questions.q: Who constructed the first recombinant DNA by linking an antibiotic resistance gene with a plasmid of Salmonella typhimurium and transferring it into E. coli?
questions.explanation: Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer made the first recombinant DNA in 1972.

questions.q: Plasmids used as vectors are best described as:
options: Extrachromosomal, self-replicating, circular DNA molecules in bacteria
questions.explanation: Plasmids are autonomously replicating circular double-stranded DNA that are used as cloning vectors.

questions.q: During agarose gel electrophoresis, DNA fragments move toward:
options: The anode, because DNA is negatively charged
The cathode, because DNA is positively charged
questions.explanation: DNA is negatively charged, so the fragments move towards the positive electrode; smaller fragments move farther.

questions.q: Separated DNA fragments in an agarose gel are stained with which compound and viewed under UV light?
questions.explanation: Ethidium bromide stains DNA and shows bright orange bands under UV radiation.

questions.q: In a stirred-tank bioreactor, the sparger is used to:
options: Maintain the pH of the culture
Introduce sterile air in the form of fine bubbles
questions.explanation: The sparger bubbles sterile air into the medium, and the stirrer mixes it for good oxygen availability.

questions.q: Bacterial cells are made competent to take up recombinant DNA by treating them with:
options: Divalent calcium ions followed by heat shock at about 42 degrees C
questions.explanation: Calcium ions increase efficiency of DNA entry through pores; a brief heat shock then lets the recombinant DNA enter.

questions.q: What is a bioreactor? Mention its main features.
questions.answer: A bioreactor is a vessel in which raw materials are biologically converted into specific products using microbial, plant or animal cells. It has an agitation system, an oxygen delivery system, a foam control system, a temperature control system, a pH control system and sampling ports.
keyPoints: Temperature and pH control, sampling ports
questions.explanation: Bioreactors allow production of large quantities of products such as enzymes.

questions.q: In pBR322, a foreign gene is inserted at the BamHI site within the tetracycline resistance gene. How can recombinant bacteria be identified?
questions.answer: Insertion at the BamHI site inactivates the tetracycline resistance gene, so recombinants are ampicillin resistant but tetracycline sensitive. Non-recombinants carry both functional genes, so they grow on both antibiotics, and the two types are separated by plating on antibiotic media.
keyPoints: Insertion inactivates the tetracycline resistance gene
questions.explanation: This is selection by insertional inactivation of an antibiotic marker.

questions.q: ELISA is based on the principle of:
questions.explanation: ELISA detects the presence of antigens or antibodies, for example for early diagnosis of HIV infection.

questions.q: A transgenic organism is one whose genome:
options: Has been altered by the introduction of a foreign gene
Is formed by cloning without any change
questions.explanation: Organisms with a manipulated genome carrying a foreign gene are called transgenic.

questions.q: The Bt gene cryIAb is used to control which pest?
questions.explanation: cryIAc and cryIIAb control cotton bollworms, while cryIAb controls the corn borer.

questions.q: Gene therapy is best described as:
options: Treatment using drugs to alter genes
Replacement of all the chromosomes of a cell
A set of methods to correct a gene defect diagnosed in a child or embryo
questions.explanation: Genes are inserted into the person's cells or tissues to correct a hereditary defect.

questions.q: Why were the A and B chains of human insulin produced separately in E. coli in the first commercial production?
options: E. coli cannot make any protein
The C peptide is essential for insulin to work
The two chains are made by different organisms
E. coli lacks the machinery to process proinsulin and remove the C peptide, so mature insulin was assembled from separate chains
questions.explanation: Mammalian proinsulin must be processed to remove the C peptide; bacteria cannot do this, so the A and B chains were made separately and linked.

questions.q: Transgenic mice carrying oncogenes are useful models because they:
options: Develop cancer with a higher probability, helping study of the disease and its treatment
questions.explanation: Mice made susceptible to cancer allow researchers to study the disease and test drugs.

questions.q: What are genetically modified organisms (GMOs)? List two uses of GM plants.
questions.answer: GMOs are plants, bacteria, fungi and animals whose genes have been altered by manipulation. GM plants can be made tolerant to abiotic stresses such as cold and drought, pest resistant, and can have enhanced nutritional value or a longer shelf life.
questions.explanation: GM crops also help reduce post-harvest losses.

questions.q: State the advantages of recombinant human insulin over insulin from animals.
questions.answer: Insulin from cattle and pigs differs slightly from human insulin and can cause allergic or immune reactions in some patients. Recombinant human insulin has the human sequence, so these reactions are avoided, and it can be produced in large quantity in bacteria.
keyPoints: Animal insulin may cause allergy or immune response
Recombinant insulin is identical to the human one
questions.explanation: Recombinant human insulin is marketed as Humulin.

questions.q: Hibernation of bears in winter is a strategy to cope with:
questions.explanation: Hibernation is a way of escaping in time from stressful cold conditions.

questions.q: An orchid growing on the branch of a mango tree is an example of:
questions.explanation: The orchid (epiphyte) benefits while the mango tree is neither harmed nor benefited.

questions.q: Cuscuta growing on a hedge plant and absorbing nutrients from it is an example of:
questions.explanation: Cuscuta is a parasitic plant that benefits at the expense of its host.

questions.q: An age pyramid with a broad base, showing a large pre-reproductive group, indicates that the population is:
questions.explanation: A triangular pyramid shows many young individuals who will enter the reproductive age, so the population will grow.

questions.q: A population of 100 individuals rises to 120 in one year with no immigration or emigration. If 30 individuals were born, how many deaths occurred?
questions.explanation: Change = births - deaths, so 20 = 30 - D, giving D = 10.

questions.q: Mammals from colder climates generally have shorter ears and limbs to minimise heat loss. This is known as:
questions.explanation: This adaptation of body shape to temperature is Allen's rule.

questions.q: Differentiate between regulators and conformers with an example of each.
questions.answer: Regulators maintain a constant internal body condition, such as temperature or osmotic concentration, despite external changes; birds and mammals are examples. Conformers cannot regulate and their internal condition changes with the surroundings; most invertebrates and fishes are examples.
keyPoints: Conformers change with the environment (e.g. most invertebrates)
questions.explanation: Regulation costs energy, but it allows wide distribution.

questions.q: How do predators help to maintain species diversity in a community? Give an example.
questions.answer: Predators keep prey populations under control, and a keystone predator reduces competition between prey species so that a competitively superior species cannot eliminate others. In the rocky intertidal of Washington, removal of the starfish Pisaster caused the loss of more than ten invertebrate species.
keyPoints: Example: Pisaster in the rocky intertidal
questions.explanation: Prickly pear in Australia was controlled by introducing a moth predator.

questions.q: Which of the following is a decomposer?
questions.explanation: Bacteria and fungi break down dead organic matter and release inorganic nutrients.

questions.q: The ultimate source of energy for almost all ecosystems on Earth is:
questions.explanation: Solar energy captured in photosynthesis drives the flow of energy through the ecosystem.

questions.q: Plants capture about what percentage of the photosynthetically active radiation (PAR)?
questions.explanation: Plants capture only 2-10 per cent of the PAR, and this small amount sustains the entire living world.

questions.q: The amount of living material (biomass) of each trophic level at a particular time is called:
questions.explanation: The standing crop is measured as the mass of living organisms (biomass) or the number in a unit area.

questions.q: Compared with the carbon cycle, the phosphorus cycle:
options: Has negligible atmospheric input, and rocks are the main reservoir
questions.explanation: Phosphorus is released by weathering of rocks, and there is no significant gaseous exchange with the atmosphere.

questions.q: Which set of processes returns carbon dioxide to the atmosphere?
options: Respiration, decomposition and burning of fossil fuels
questions.explanation: CO2 is released by respiration of organisms, decomposition of organic matter and combustion of fuels.

questions.q: What is ecological succession? Differentiate between primary and secondary succession.
questions.answer: Ecological succession is the gradual and fairly predictable change in the species composition of a given area over time, ending in a climax community. Primary succession starts in a lifeless area like bare rock with no soil, whereas secondary succession starts in an area that has lost a community but retains soil, so it is faster.
keyPoints: Gradual change in species composition leading to climax
questions.explanation: Examples of secondary succession are abandoned farms and burnt forests.

questions.q: Explain why energy flow in an ecosystem is unidirectional and why food chains are usually short.
questions.answer: Energy captured by producers flows to higher trophic levels and cannot return to the sun or to the producers, as much is lost as heat. Only about 10 per cent is transferred to the next level, so very little remains after 3 to 4 levels, which limits the length of food chains.
keyPoints: Energy lost as heat at each level, cannot be reused
Only about 10% transferred to the next level
Little energy remains beyond 3-4 trophic levels
questions.explanation: Energy flow obeys the laws of thermodynamics.

questions.q: How does species richness generally change as one moves from the poles towards the equator?
options: It decreases and then remains constant
questions.explanation: Species diversity generally decreases from the equator towards the poles, which is the latitudinal gradient.

questions.q: The IUCN Red List provides information on:
options: The conservation status of species, including threatened ones
The forest area of each country
questions.explanation: The Red List categorises species according to their risk of extinction.

questions.q: Gametes of threatened species can be preserved for long periods by cryopreservation at about:
questions.explanation: Cryopreservation in liquid nitrogen at -196 degrees C stops cellular activity so that gametes can be stored.

questions.q: Which of the following animals became extinct in the last few hundred years?
questions.explanation: The dodo of Mauritius is one of the species extinct in recent history; the Steller's sea cow and quagga are others.

questions.q: When a host fish species becomes extinct, its specialised parasites also disappear. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Co-extinction occurs when the extinction of one species causes the extinction of another that depends on it.

questions.q: The medicinal plant Rauwolfia vomitoria shows variation in the potency and concentration of reserpine in different Himalayan ranges. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Differences within a single species are genetic diversity.

questions.q: Name the three levels of biodiversity and give one example of each.
questions.answer: Genetic diversity is variation within a species, such as the many varieties of rice or of mango. Species diversity is the variety of species in a region, such as the Western Ghats having more amphibian species than the Eastern Ghats. Ecological diversity is the variety of ecosystems, such as deserts, rain forests and mangroves.
questions.explanation: India has about 50,000 genetically different strains of rice.

questions.q: Why should biodiversity be conserved? Explain the narrowly utilitarian, broadly utilitarian and ethical arguments.
questions.answer: The narrowly utilitarian argument says that humans get food, firewood, fibre, medicines and industrial products from biodiversity. The broadly utilitarian argument says that ecosystems provide services such as oxygen, pollination and climate regulation. The ethical argument says every species has intrinsic value and we have a moral duty to pass it to future generations.
keyPoints: Ethical: intrinsic value of species, duty to future generations
questions.explanation: These three arguments are used to justify conservation.
